newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban propose truce, rivals blast road.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban propose truce, rivals blast road.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia renewed a ceasefire offer to its weakened opponents on Monday but ruled out any power-sharing deal.

"We have been keen on the idea of a ceasefire from the very beginning," acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told Reuters. "We want an immediate ceasefire now, with an exchange of prisoners to take place on the first day it is enforced."
He said an anti-Taleban alliance led by former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood and General Abdul Rashid Dostum must not use a truce to buy time to strengthen its military position.
"There should be a guarantee from the opposition that they will not regroup or reinforce their troops during the ceasefire," Mutaqi said.

The Taleban has inflicted major defeats on Masood and Dostum north of Kabul in the past two weeks, recapturing positions the Islamic militia had initially taken -- but later lost -- shortly after capturing the Afghan capital on September 27.
Troops loyal to Dostum have blown up a portion of the Salang highway to prevent a possible further advance by the Taleban northward, travellers arriving in Kabul said.
"Tens of cars with passengers intending to go north through the Salang tunnel were sent back to Kabul as Taleban fighters told them the road was no more open for traffic," a bus driver said.
A Taleban thrust on Thursday pushed Masood's forces to the Panjsher valley and Dostum's troops to the vital Salang Pass, which passes through the Hindukush mountains.
The nearly three-km (two-mile) Salang tunnel, 120 km (75 miles) north of Kabul, is the main route to northern provinces and beyond to Central Asia.
The travellers said Dostum's fighters had blown up the road five km (three miles) south of the tunnel.
The latest Taleban ceasefire offer followed the conclusion of talks among Afghan factions in Tehran that were boycotted by the Taleban, which accused Iran of not being a neutral party.
"The participants called for an immediate ceasefire, the creation of a safe and secure environment in Kabul and the exchange of POWs," said a statement at the end of the talks.
"The sharing of power by all parties in the structure of the national government is indispensable," it added.
However, Mutaqi made clear that the Taleban was not interested in sharing power with hostile factions.
"Our government represents every province of Afghanistan and power, whether military or administrative, is shared by delegates of people from all over Afghanistan," he said.
"Anyone who is not a criminal can take part in the government," Mutaqi added.
The Taleban administration has frequently denounced Dostum and Masood as criminals plundering and oppressing the country.
The Taleban, who sprang from religious schools for Afghan refugees in Pakistan, aim to spread their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law across Afghanistan.
Iran, long suspicious of the Sunni Moslem radicals, still recognises the former government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani, but denies actively supporting any Afghan faction.
"Taleban missed their chance of an intra-Afghan dialogue for a peaceful settlement of the crisis," Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said after the Tehran talks.
